Amend

uh-MEND — contains 'mend,' as in fixing something; to amend is to mend a flaw in a rule or plan. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To amend to make something better by changing or correcting it.

Lawmakers voted to amend the outdated regulation after years of complaints from small business owners.

Worked Example

A club's rulebook bans anyone under sixteen from voting, even though many younger members have been active for years. After a long discussion, the members agree to change that one rule so any member who has attended ten meetings can vote, regardless of age.

Changing a rule to fix a flaw and make it better is exactly what it means to amend it. Unlike 'abolish,' which means to get rid of something completely, amend means to improve or revise part of it.

How Amend Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

revise

revise: to change or update something, often a document

reform

reform: to improve by making changes, especially to a system

correct

correct: to fix a mistake or error

Antonyms

worsen

worsen: to make something more bad or severe

preserve

preserve: to keep something exactly as it is

How Strong Is It? — adjust → amend → overhaul

adjust vs. amend

adjust vs. amend: Adjust is weaker than amend — adjusting something is a small tweak, while amending it usually means a more formal, deliberate correction to fix a real flaw.

overhaul vs. amend

overhaul vs. amend: Overhaul is stronger than amend: amending a policy fixes one flawed part, but overhauling it means rebuilding the entire thing from the ground up.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — a- (ad-)

prefix — a- (ad-): to (Latin)

root — -mend-

root — -mend-: fault, flaw, blemish (Latin (menda))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin emendare combined e- (out) with menda ('a fault') to mean 'to remove a fault.' To amend something is, at its root, to correct a flaw in it.

Use the root in a new word: mend

Use the root in a new word: mend: She sat by the fire to mend the torn sleeve of her coat.
